documents.title: Guidelines for the Use of Generative AI Tools
documents.summary: A 2023 letter from the provost and two vice presidents encourages the community to experiment with AI and sets six general guidelines on confidential data, public-by-default input, academic integrity, bias and verification, credentials and procurement. Course-level permission is left to instructors, whom it asks to give clear instructions and attribution rules.
documents.stance_why: The letter says "We encourage you to experiment with AI tools" but sets no rule for coursework itself: "Faculty members are expected to provide clear instructions on the permitted use of generative AI tools" and students "are expected to follow their instructors' guidelines." The decision is handed to instructors, so delegates. Reconciliation: coder A coded delegates and coder B encourage. The letter encourages experimentation but sets no rule for coursework and hands permitted use to instructors ("expected to follow their instructors' guidelines"); its restrictions concern data and credentials. The codebook gives delegates for documents that hand the decision to instructors, so delegates; the encouraging language is kept at unit level (P02, P56, encourage).

units.why: The letter says "We encourage you to experiment with AI tools," an explicit welcome of AI use addressed to the whole community, so it is a default-permissive stance (P02), encourage, general phase.
units.anchor: We encourage you to experiment with AI tools.

units.why: "this technology will transform how we learn, teach, conduct research, and carry out daily tasks" is an impact claim with no rule, so informs. P87 (benefits) is the nearest type but the sentence says "transform," not a named benefit.

units.frag_start: While its precise impacts are unknown
units.fit_note: States that AI will transform learning, teaching, research and daily tasks and that impacts are unknown; a general impact claim rather than a named benefit.
units.resolution_why: Only coder A coded this sentence ("this technology will transform how we learn, teach, conduct research, and carry out daily tasks"). Coder B skipped it. The source has the sentence, and it is a statement about AI's effect on learning and teaching, so it is kept as an informs unit. Type P87 is kept with A's fit note because the sentence is a general impact claim, not a named benefit.

units.resolution_why: Coder A coded modality informs, coder B must. The source reads "please adhere to the following general guidelines, which align with existing university policies". The anchor is the clause saying the guidelines align with existing policy, which describes the guidelines rather than commanding anything; the duty to adhere is stated in the lead-in, not in the anchor. Final: informs. Type P77 (both coders) kept; B's note that the sentence also names safety and security commitments is retained.

units.resolution_why: Coders differed on actor (A student, B all) and phase (A course-start, B general). The source speaks to "you" (the student): "How and whether instructors permit you to use AI writing tools at Yale will vary widely", so actor student. It states the delegation principle rather than communicating a course's rules at the start of a course, so phase general (B). P04 and informs agree.

units.why: "Always check with your instructor before using these tools to produce your Yale coursework" tells students to ask before using AI: P10.
units.anchor: Always check with your instructor before using these tools

units.why: "the standard penalty is two semesters of suspension" for cheating states a concrete penalty; it names cheating, not AI, and applies to AI misuse only through the AI note that calls it a breach of integrity: P37.
units.anchor: the standard penalty is two semesters of suspension
units.frag_start: Yale regards cheating as a serious
units.fit_note: About cheating generally; does not name AI.
units.resolution_why: Only coder A coded "the standard penalty is two semesters of suspension" for cheating. The sentence is in the source and does not name AI, but the AI note in the same regulation classes unattributed or unauthorized AI use as a violation or breach of academic integrity, so the stated penalty is the sanction that applies. Kept as P37 (informs, when-misuse) with A's fit note that it is about cheating generally. Coder A's two rationale units from the integrity preface ("doing the very work of synthesis", "turn in someone else's work ... giving away the very substance of their educations") were dropped: neither mentions AI, and they describe why cheating in general harms learning, not an AI policy.
